research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. API and reported event

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and creates secure-socket factories or `SSLEngine` instances. The reported event concerns the **first argument** of `SSLContext.init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)`: the key managers supplying local authentication keys. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The detector’s description of a null key-manager argument requires qualification:

- The `SSLContext.init` API documentation permits null and says installed providers are searched for the highest-priority appropriate factory.
- Oracle’s JSSE guide separately says that a null `KeyManager[]` results in an **empty key manager** for the initialized context. It distinguishes this from the internal default context, for which default key and trust managers are created.

Those descriptions are not identical. The sources do not establish that every provider uses the platform’s configured default identity when `init` receives a null key-manager array. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

### 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle documents null arguments as API-valid; it does **not** prescribe universal remediation merely because `km` is null. For local authentication, its guide says to initialize the context with suitable key managers. It documents obtaining them from an appropriately initialized `KeyManagerFactory`, using a keystore and password or provider-specific parameters, then retrieving its key-manager array. A concrete key-manager implementation is also an API-supported option. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

A null trust-manager array and a null random source are also documented as valid defaults. Only the first manager of a particular implementation type in an array is used. For raw sockets or engines, Oracle separately advises checking the peer’s credentials and describes endpoint identification during the handshake. These are separate concerns from selecting local key managers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html

### 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted formats:** The cited API and JSSE guidance describe supplying key material, but do not prescribe a persisted-format conversion as a consequence of changing the `init` argument. The appropriate keystore and factory initialization remain provider-dependent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
- **Wire behavior:** Changing available key managers can change which local credentials can be selected for authentication. The sources do not state that this change alone requires a new TLS wire format or give a universal migration path. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
- **Platform support:** `SSLContext` has existed since Java 1.4. The Java 21 API requires support for `TLSv1.2`; other protocol support must be checked against the implementation. Oracle documents TLS 1.3 in JDK 11, but that does not establish support in every older provider or platform. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- **Protocol compatibility:** The rule’s `getInstance` string restriction is not a check of enabled or negotiated versions. Oracle documents that enabled versions can vary by context algorithm, mode, configuration and JDK release; standard names such as `TLSv1.3` can support other versions too. A `getInstance("TLS")` call alone does not establish legacy negotiation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/oracle-providers.html?utm_source=openai))

Sources:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/oracle-providers.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/migrate/security-updates.html

### 4. Exact CrySL rule and source limits

The supplied rule declares `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` as its governed type. Its matching clause for the reported initialization event is:

```text
	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;
```

It declares `km`, `tm` and `random` as `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]` and `SecureRandom`, respectively. Thus the clause specifies a **three-parameter call**, rather than an unconstrained parameter list. It then requires the predicates `generatedKeyManagers[km]`, `generatedTrustManagers[tm]` and `randomized[random]`. The file does not itself say that null is forbidden. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The same file declares:

- `getInstance` events with one protocol argument or a protocol plus an unconstrained second argument; the protocol constraint is the literal set `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`.
- Zero- or two-argument `createSSLEngine` events.
- A forbidden zero-argument `getDefault` event, mapped to `Get`.
- The order `Get, Init, Engine?`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Name-only matching:** The rule is type-scoped to `SSLContext` and specifies event parameter shapes; it does not state a rule matching an unrelated receiver merely because its method shares one of those names. The file alone does not document a detector implementation’s resolution behavior, so it cannot rule out an implementation-specific matching error. The `getInstance` and `getDefault` API methods are static; `init` and `createSSLEngine` are instance methods. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Rule source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl

**Unresolved:** The linked rule’s key-manager requirement appears under `REQUIRES`, whereas its explicit `CONSTRAINTS` section contains the protocol whitelist. The file does not explain the supplied `UnsatisfiedConstraint` diagnostic label or prove which compiled rule artifact produced it. The linked URL tracks a mutable branch; the supplied SHA-256 and detector version were not independently verified here. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))
